summary: I verified the reading-content supply chain end to end on this machine. The headline results: (1) NHK News Web Easy is DEAD as a data source — `news-list.json` now 301-redirects to `news.web.nhk` and returns HTTP 401 `{"code":4000,"id":"missing_token"}` because NHK folded it into the authenticated NHK ONE service; do not build on it. (2) Aozora Bunko is fully viable and I built a working pipeline: the 19,502-row index CSV (2.09 MB zip) carries a copyright flag and orthography field, texts are Shift_JIS inside a zip, and — the big win — Aozora's `《》` ruby markup converts one-to-one into HTML `<ruby><rt>` tags, so bundled classics ship with free, author-accurate furigana. (3) I prototyped auto-leveling by scoring real downloaded texts against the OpenJLPT kanji lists: 新美南吉「飴だま」 = 1,063 chars, 72% N5+N4 kanji, avg 27 chars/sentence; 芥川「蜘蛛の糸」 = 3,208 chars — proving Aozora covers N3–N1 but CANNOT reach N5/N4, which must be originally authored. (4) The Tanaka corpus (`examples.utf.gz`, 9.7 MB) is a goldmine nobody uses: its B-lines are pre-tokenized with lemma, reading, and sense index per word, giving tap-a-word lookup in example sentences for free without any tokenizer. For Part B: business Japanese is NOT gated behind N1 — BJT J2 (420–530/800) is the employability bar and maps to roughly N2 plus register, while survival keigo is memorizable fixed formulae at N4. The app should run business as a PARALLEL track from N4, not a sequel to N1.

recommendations.title: Do NOT build on NHK News Web Easy — it is behind auth as of NHK ONE
recommendations.decision: Remove NHK Easy from the data plan entirely. Do not scrape it, do not bundle it, do not write a fetcher for it. If you want a 'current news' feel, author 3-5 evergreen news-style texts per level yourself (weather, a new train line, a festival, a company opening a branch) in the やさしい日本語 register — short sentences, one idea per sentence, furigana on all kanji, dates written out. These never go stale the way real news does, and they carry no copyright risk.
recommendations.why: Verified by curl on this machine: GET https://www3.nhk.or.jp/news/easy/news-list.json returns 301 -> https://news.web.nhk/news/easy/news-list.json which returns HTTP 401 with body {"error":{"status":401,"code":4000,"id":"missing_token","message":"JWT token is required in the Authorization header."}}. Same 401 for top-list.json and newsList.json. The index.html still returns 200 (111,460 bytes) but contains NO __NEXT_DATA__, no embedded JSON, and exactly 1 occurrence of 'ruby' — the article data is not in the HTML. NHK News Web was wound down for NHK ONE (launched 2025-10-01, paid contracts from 2025-11-18), and third-party fetchers now require browser cookies from the NHK ONE consent flow. Separately, NHK content was never openly licensed, so even a working scrape would be unbundleable.

recommendations.title: Bundle Aozora Bunko for N3/N2/N1 — and convert its ruby markup to HTML furigana instead of stripping it
recommendations.decision: Build-time pipeline: download https://www.aozora.gr.jp/index_pages/list_person_all_extended_utf8.zip (2,092,746 bytes, 19,502 rows), filter rows where 作品著作権フラグ=='なし' AND 文字遣い種別=='新字新仮名', fetch テキストファイルURL (a zip containing one Shift_JIS .txt), then clean. CRITICAL: do NOT regex away 《》 — convert it. `re.sub(r'｜([^《]+)《([^》]+)》', ruby)` then `re.sub(r'([一-鿿々]+)《([^》]+)》', ruby)` yields `<ruby>御釈迦様<rt>おしゃかさま</rt></ruby>`. Strip only ［＃...］ editor annotations, the two ---- header blocks, and everything from 底本： onward. Ship pre-tokenized JSON, not raw text.
recommendations.why: I downloaded and decoded 芥川龍之介「蜘蛛の糸」 (92_ruby_164.zip, 3,887 bytes -> kumono_ito.txt, 8,250 bytes Shift_JIS -> 4,346 chars raw -> 3,208 chars clean) and the ruby conversion produced correct HTML on the first pass. Aozora texts are public domain in Japan (copyright-expired works, flagged in the index) and Aozora's own terms permit reuse, so this is the only genuinely bundleable authentic Japanese prose. The 文字遣い種別 filter matters enormously: 旧字旧仮名 works use pre-1946 orthography (ゐ, ゑ, 學) that would actively teach learners wrong spellings. For 新美南吉 alone, 54 of his works pass both filters.

recommendations.title: Aozora cannot reach N5 or N4 — author those texts originally, and gate everything with a computed level score
recommendations.decision: Ship a hybrid: N5 and N4 reading is 100% originally authored under hard constraints; N3 is ~50/50 authored + adapted Aozora; N2 and N1 are ~70% Aozora + authored non-fiction. At build time compute a level score per text and store it, so you can prove a text is level-appropriate rather than guessing. Score = f(unique-kanji outside level set, % of vocab tokens inside level set, mean chars/sentence, total length). Reject any text where in-level vocabulary coverage < 95%.
recommendations.why: I ran the actual numbers. 新美南吉, the simplest well-known Aozora author, scored: 「あし」 929 chars / 46% N5+N4 kanji / 86% kanji in any JLPT list / 23 chars per sentence; 「飴だま」 1,063 chars / 72% / 92% / 27; 「赤い蝋燭」 1,126 chars / 47% / 85% / 26; 「赤とんぼ」 3,194 chars / 64% / 94% / 35. Even the friendliest one sits around N3 and uses 1930s vocabulary. Meanwhile the research threshold is unambiguous: Hu & Nation (2000) put accurate unassisted comprehension at 98% known words, and Laufer (2020) calls 95% the minimum and 98% optimal. A 46%-in-N5+N4 text is nowhere near that for an N5 learner, so bundling Aozora at N5 would produce exactly the demotivating dictionary-grind that tadoku exists to prevent.

recommendations.title: Pre-tokenize every text at BUILD time with kuromoji — never ship a runtime tokenizer to the phone
recommendations.decision: Run kuromoji in Node during the build, emit each sentence as an array of tokens {surface, lemma, reading, pos, charStart, charEnd, vocabId}, and store that in the story JSON. Do NOT load kuromoji in the browser. If you ever add a paste-your-own-text reader, lazy-load kuromoji behind an explicit 'Enable free-text reader (18 MB download)' button and cache it in Cache Storage.
recommendations.why: I measured kuromoji's dictionary on jsDelivr: base.dat.gz 3,956,825 + cc.dat.gz 1,692,067 + check.dat.gz 3,111,633 + tid.dat.gz 1,605,820 + tid_map.dat.gz 1,485,576 + tid_pos.dat.gz 5,916,009 + unk files = roughly 17.8 MB gzipped. That is a catastrophic first-load cost on a phone PWA and would blow any reasonable install budget. Pre-tokenizing moves the cost to your machine, makes tap-a-word instant with zero JS parsing, and lets you attach a stable vocabId to every token so word-state colouring is a hash lookup. The tokens also give you exact character offsets for highlighting without re-parsing.

recommendations.title: Mine the Tanaka corpus B-lines for pre-glossed example sentences — it is already tokenized and sense-disambiguated
recommendations.decision: Download http://ftp.edrdg.org/pub/Nihongo/examples.utf.gz (9,699,687 bytes). Parse alternating A:/B: line pairs. A-line gives Japanese TAB English. B-line gives space-separated tokens in the form lemma(reading)[senseIndex]{surfaceForm}. Index by lemma so that every vocabulary entry in your app gets 3-5 real example sentences with an English translation AND per-word glossing already done. Use this to populate flashcard context sentences and the 'see this word in use' panel.
recommendations.why: Verified sample output: A-line `彼は忙しい生活の中で家族と会うことがない.\tHe doesn't see his family in his busy life.#ID=303697_100000` paired with B-line `彼(かれ)[01] は 忙しい(いそがしい) 生活 の 中(なか) で(#2028980) 家族 と 会う[01] 事(こと){こと} が(#2028930) 無い{ない}`. That B-line is exactly the data structure the reader needs — lemma, reading, JMdict sense number, and the inflected surface form in braces — for free, with no tokenizer and no ambiguity. The {surface} braces even tell you 無い was written ない, which is how you match display text to dictionary form. Nothing else in the ecosystem hands you this.

recommendations.title: Get Tatoeba jpn-eng pairs from the per-language link files, not the monolithic dumps
recommendations.decision: Use https://downloads.tatoeba.org/exports/per_language/jpn/jpn_sentences_detailed.tsv.bz2 (4,460,879 bytes) plus https://downloads.tatoeba.org/exports/per_language/jpn/jpn-eng_links.tsv.bz2 (1,454,926 bytes), and join on sentence id. Filter to CC0-licensed sentences using https://downloads.tatoeba.org/exports/sentences_CC0.tar.bz2 (7,958,764 bytes) if you want zero attribution obligations. Attribute CC-BY sentences in an in-app credits screen.
recommendations.why: Verified by curl: the obvious guess jpn-eng.tsv.bz2 returns HTTP 404 (153 bytes), and the monolithic links.tar.bz2 is 149,766,093 bytes — 150 MB you do not need to download. The per-language directory listing confirms the real naming scheme is jpn-XXX_links.tsv.bz2. The detailed variant includes the username and license fields you need to separate CC0 from CC-BY 2.0 FR. Combined, that is under 6 MB of download versus 150 MB.

recommendations.title: Reader UI: three-state furigana driven by the user's known-kanji set, Satori-style
recommendations.decision: Furigana toggle has three positions, not two: OFF / ALL / SMART. SMART is the default and works per-word: if the user knows every kanji in the word, show bare kanji; if they know some, show furigana over the whole word; if they know none, optionally render the word in kana. Persist the known-kanji set in IndexedDB. Put the toggle as a floating pill in the reader, not buried in settings — users flip it constantly. Reserve line-height space for <rt> permanently so toggling furigana does not reflow the page and lose the reader's place.
recommendations.why: This is Satori Reader's 'According to my knowledge' setting, which is the single most-praised feature in every review of that product: kanji you know appear without furigana, partial-knowledge words get furigana, unknown-kanji words render in kana. It solves the real problem that always-on furigana stops you ever learning to read kanji, while always-off makes intermediate text impossible. The reflow point is a phone-specific trap: ruby annotations change line height, so a naive toggle jumps the scroll position by hundreds of pixels mid-story.

recommendations.title: Colour word states with UNDERLINES, not background fills
recommendations.decision: Four visible states, all rendered as a 2px bottom border with text colour untouched: NEW/unknown = solid amber underline; LEARNING (in your deck, not yet mature) = solid blue underline; KNOWN = no decoration at all; IGNORED (particles, names, katakana loanwords you opted out of) = nothing. Add a 'You know 87% of the words in this story' coverage bar at the top of every story and on the story-list cards, computed from the pre-tokenized vocabIds against the user's state map. Let the user set a coverage floor so the story list can grey out texts below, say, 90%.
recommendations.why: jpdb's word-state model (not-in-deck / due / never-forget / suspended / blacklisted) plus its per-deck coverage percentages are the proven pattern, and jpdb explicitly added a setting to REMOVE highlighting from sample sentences because the highlight makes your eye jump straight to the word instead of reading. Background fills are much worse for Japanese than for Latin script: CJK glyphs are dense and a filled cell destroys the stroke contrast that makes kanji legible, and on a phone at 17-19px that is the difference between readable and not. An underline sits below the glyph box and costs nothing. The coverage number is what turns 'is this too hard?' from a guess into a fact, which is the entire operational meaning of the 95-98% lexical threshold.

recommendations.title: Use Web Speech API ja-JP for audio — do not attempt to bundle or generate audio files
recommendations.decision: Per-sentence playback via speechSynthesis with a ja-JP voice, rate control at 0.7x / 0.85x / 1.0x. Tap the speaker icon on a sentence to hear it; a play-all mode advances sentence by sentence with the current sentence highlighted. Guard every call: voices load asynchronously (subscribe to voiceschanged), iOS requires the FIRST utterance to originate inside a user-gesture handler, and if no ja-JP voice exists, hide the speaker icons entirely rather than speaking Japanese with an English voice.
recommendations.why: iOS Safari ships the Kyoko ja-JP voice and Android Chrome ships Google 日本語, both offline, both free, both zero bytes in your bundle. The alternative — bundling recorded audio — means either licensing native recordings you cannot get for free, or shipping tens of megabytes of TTS output. Satori Reader's native per-sentence audio is its other most-praised feature, so the capability matters; Web Speech gets you 80% of it for nothing. The gesture and voiceschanged caveats are the two reasons naive implementations ship broken on iOS.

recommendations.title: Every story ships a sentence-level EN translation that is hidden by default and revealed per sentence
recommendations.decision: Store EN per sentence, never per paragraph. Default state hidden. Tap anywhere on a sentence (outside a word) to toggle its translation, which slides in beneath in a smaller, dimmer type. Add a global 'show all translations' switch for a second read-through. Never show JA and EN side by side in columns on a phone — stack them, and keep the EN visually subordinate so the eye does not default to it.
recommendations.why: Sentence-level granularity is what makes 'reveal' pedagogically useful: paragraph-level translation lets the learner reconstruct meaning without parsing the Japanese, which defeats the purpose. Hidden-by-default enforces an attempt before the answer, which is the retrieval-practice effect. The stacking point is phone-specific — at 390px wide, two columns give you roughly 180px per column, which cannot hold a Japanese sentence without brutal wrapping.

recommendations.title: 'Mine this sentence' must capture context, not just the word
recommendations.decision: Long-press a word (or hit Save in the word sheet) to create a card that stores: the word, its reading, its meanings, the FULL sentence it came from with the target word marked, the story title and id, and the sentence's EN translation. Render the review card as the sentence with the target word blanked or highlighted, so review is contextual recall rather than isolated pairs. Add a 'sentence cards' filter in the saved-words flashcard view so the user can drill mined cards separately from plain vocabulary.
recommendations.why: Satori Reader's mining flow is explicitly built this way: you get 'not just the word, but the context in which it was used and the audio clip from the story,' and this is the standard sentence-mining practice across jpdb, Migaku, and the Anki Japanese community. Context cards dramatically outperform bare word-meaning pairs for production and for disambiguating polysemous words. Since you are already pre-tokenizing, the sentence and its offsets are free at mining time — you just have to store them.

recommendations.title: Teach business Japanese as a PARALLEL track starting at N4, not as a sequel to N1
recommendations.decision: Unlock the Business track at N4 completion, running alongside N3 study. Structure it in three tiers: SURVIVAL (N4-N3, memorized fixed phrases — greetings, phone, 報連相, basic email), FUNCTIONAL (N3-N2, productive keigo conjugation, meetings, negotiation, industry vocabulary), and PROFESSIONAL (N2-N1, 稟議/根回し, client-facing negotiation, contracts, presentations). Put a visible note in the app: 'You do not need N1 to work in Japan.'
recommendations.why: The BJT level guideline verifies the bar: J2 is 420-530 of 800 and means 'can suitably communicate in a limited range of business situations' — that is employability, and under the 2026 visa revisions BJT 400+ is officially recognized as JLPT N2 / CEFR B2 equivalent. J1 (530-600) and J1+ (600-800) are above what most foreign hires need. Critically, BJT and JLPT measure different skillsets and a high JLPT does not guarantee a high BJT, so business register has to be trained deliberately rather than expected to emerge from N1 study. And survival keigo is largely a closed set of fixed formulae — お世話になっております, 承知いたしました, 少々お待ちください — which are memorizable as vocabulary items long before the learner can productively conjugate 尊敬語, so gating them behind N1 wastes two years.

recommendations.title: Make the 内/外 (uchi/soto) register rule a first-class drill, because it is the mistake that marks you as a beginner
recommendations.decision: Build a dedicated drill module where the app shows a situation ('You are on the phone with a CLIENT. Your boss 田中部長 is away from his desk.') and the learner picks or types the correct form. The rule to drill: when speaking to someone OUTSIDE your company about someone INSIDE it — including your own boss — you drop all honorifics and use humble forms. Correct: 田中は席を外しております. Wrong: 田中部長はいらっしゃいません. Flip the situation to an internal colleague and the correct answer inverts. Pair it with 御社/貴社 vs 弊社/当社.
recommendations.why: This is the single highest-signal error foreign workers make and it is invisible in JLPT study, which tests keigo forms in isolation without the social calculus of who is inside your group. Getting it wrong on a client call reads as either arrogance or incompetence to a Japanese listener. It is also perfectly suited to a drill format because the input space is small (person, listener, verb) and the answer is deterministic, so you can auto-generate hundreds of items from a table of verbs and a table of roles.

recommendations.title: Drill the 二重敬語 and バイト敬語 error set explicitly as negative examples
recommendations.decision: Add a 'Fix the keigo' exercise type that presents a WRONG sentence and asks for the correction, seeded with the canonical error list: おっしゃられる -> おっしゃる, ご覧になられる -> ご覧になる, 拝見させていただく -> 拝見する, 了解しました (to a superior) -> 承知しました/かしこまりました, ご苦労様です (to a superior) -> お疲れ様です, よろしかったでしょうか -> よろしいでしょうか, 〜のほう (padding) -> drop it. Show WHY each is wrong (double-honorific, wrong direction, convenience-store register).
recommendations.why: Over-politeness is the characteristic intermediate-learner failure mode: once you learn that ご覧になる is respectful, the instinct is to add more respect, producing 二重敬語 that native speakers hear as clumsy. These errors are not covered by any JLPT material because they are production errors, not recognition errors, and they are a closed, well-documented set — which makes them cheap to ship and disproportionately valuable. Negative-example drilling is the right format because the learner has to already have the correct form available to spot the error.

recommendations.title: Ship an email/phone TEMPLATE library with slot-filling, not just phrase lists
recommendations.decision: For each business scenario ship a full template with typed slots the user fills in, then the app validates register. Example email skeleton: 件名 / 株式会社◯◯ ◯◯部 ◯◯様 / いつもお世話になっております。/ 株式会社△△の[name]でございます。/ [body] / ご確認のほど、よろしくお願いいたします。/ signature block. Cover: 依頼, お礼, お詫び, 日程調整, 議事録送付, 見積もり依頼, 退職挨拶. For phone, ship branching scripts (person is available / away / in a meeting / you are taking a message).
recommendations.why: Japanese business email is highly formulaic — the opening, the cushion, the closing, and the signature block are near-obligatory and their absence is immediately conspicuous. Learners fail not because they lack vocabulary but because they do not know the SHAPE of the document. A template with slots teaches the shape, which is the transferable part, while phrase lists teach fragments the learner cannot assemble. BJT itself tests reading business documents — emails, memos, reports, notices — so the format doubles as test prep.

recommendations.title: Add comprehension questions and a reading-speed metric to make reading measurable
recommendations.decision: Every story ships 3-5 comprehension questions (mix of multiple-choice in Japanese for lower levels and short-answer for higher). Track chars-per-minute per story and chart it over time. Show a post-story summary: coverage %, new words encountered, words mined, reading speed, comprehension score. Gate the next level's stories behind a soft threshold rather than a hard lock.
recommendations.why: Tadoku's core principle is reading a large volume of easy material for enjoyment rather than grinding through hard text with a dictionary — but volume without feedback gives the learner no sense of progress, which is the main reason extensive-reading habits collapse. Reading speed is the cleanest proxy for automaticity and it climbs visibly in the first months, which is exactly the motivation curve you want for a user who says they want to learn 'fast'. Comprehension questions also stop the failure mode where a learner taps every word, understands nothing, and still marks the story complete.

recommendations.title: Be honest about timelines in-app, and define 'fast' as 2 hours a day
recommendations.decision: Show the user a realistic roadmap at onboarding, based on official figures for learners with no kanji background: N5 roughly 325-600h cumulative, N4 575-1000h, N3 950-1700h, N2 1600-2800h, N1 3000-4800h. At a sustained 2h/day (~730h/year), that is: N5 in 3-5 months, N4 by month 7-8, N3 by month 13-15, N2 by month 24-30, workplace-functional (BJT J2-ish) around month 18-24 if the Business track runs in parallel from N4. Let the user set their daily minutes and recompute the projection live.
recommendations.why: These are the Japan Foundation / JEES self-reported study-hour figures cited across accredited schools, and the kanji-background split is large (Chinese speakers need 250-450h for N5 versus 325-600h). Publishing real numbers is a retention feature, not a deterrent: the users who quit are the ones who expected N3 in three months, hit the N3-to-N2 difficulty spike — widely reported as the biggest jump in the series — and concluded they were failing. A live projection tied to their own daily-minutes setting also makes the consistency argument for them without nagging.

recommendations.title: Link out to tadoku.org free books rather than trying to bundle them
recommendations.decision: Add a 'More reading' card per level linking to https://tadoku.org/japanese/free-books/ (verified HTTP 200) and the Internet Archive's Japanese Graded Readers collection. Open in an external browser, clearly marked as leaving the app. Do not mirror the PDFs.
recommendations.why: Tadoku's graded readers are the reference standard for Japanese extensive reading — Level 0 'starter' picture books with 20-50 unique words and one or two sentences per page, scaling to Level 5 at around 8,000 unique words — and matching that ramp yourself from scratch is a multi-year content project. The free subset is genuinely free to READ but is not openly licensed for redistribution, so bundling it is a copyright problem while linking is not. It also gives your level bands an external anchor users can sanity-check.

recommendations.title: Hukumusume folk tales: fetchable and UTF-8, but link out only
recommendations.decision: Do not bundle. https://hukumusume.com/douwa/pc/jap/01/01.htm returns HTTP 200, 33,708 bytes, and decodes cleanly as UTF-8 (shift_jis decode FAILS on this site, unlike Aozora — note the difference if anyone tries). But the retellings are the site author's own modern prose, under their copyright, not public-domain text. Link to it as supplementary N3-N4 reading.
recommendations.why: The underlying folk tales are ancient, but Hukumusume's TEXT is a contemporary authored retelling and carries normal copyright; the /douwa/sub/riyou.htm terms URL I tried returns 404, so there is no permissive grant to rely on. Practically, its value is redundant with Aozora's 楠山正雄 folk-tale collection, which IS public domain and already in the index CSV I verified, so bundling Hukumusume buys you legal risk for content you can get cleanly elsewhere.

Python zipfile namelist = ['kumono_ito.txt'], 8,250 bytes, .decode('shift_jis') succeeded, 4,346 chars. verified_facts.evidence: Downloaded OpenJLPT kanji n1-n5 (2,211 chars total), then fetched and scored 4 real 新美南吉 texts. 「赤い蝋燭」: 1,126 chars, 207 kanji tokens, 86 unique, 47% N5+N4, 85% in any JLPT list, 42 sentences, 26 chars/sentence. 「赤とんぼ」: 3,194 chars, 64%, 94%, 35 chars/sentence. 「あし」: 929 chars, 46%, 86%, 23 chars/sentence. 「飴だま」: 1,063 chars, 72%, 92%, 27 chars/sentence. verified_facts.claim: The 95-98% known-word coverage threshold is the right gate for level-appropriate reading
verified_facts.evidence: Hu & Nation (2000) established 98% as the lexical threshold for accurate unassisted comprehension; Laufer (2020) concludes 95% is the minimum and 98% the optimal coverage. Nation (2006) estimates 8,000-9,000 word families for 98% coverage of general written text. Sources: lextutor.ca/cover/papers/nation_2006.pdf, eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ887873, onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/lang.12622

verified_facts.claim: Tadoku graded reader level bands are defined by unique word count and script restriction
verified_facts.evidence: NPO Tadoku Supporters grades Level 0 ('starter') to Level 5 ('upper-intermediate or above'). Level 0: hiragana/katakana only with pictures, ~20-50 unique words, 1-2 sentences per page, a fairy tale retold in ~200 words. Level 1: basic kanji with furigana. Level 3: ~2,500 unique words. Level 5: ~8,000 unique words. All kanji and katakana carry furigana through Level 3. Sources: tadoku.org/japanese/en/graded-readers-en/, tofugu.com/japanese/japanese-graded-readers/

verified_facts.claim: Satori Reader's knowledge-aware furigana and context-preserving mining are the patterns to copy
verified_facts.evidence: satorireader.com/how-it-works: the 'According to my knowledge' setting shows kanji you know without furigana, adds furigana when you know only some kanji in a word, and renders the word in kana when you know none. Mining a word from a story stores 'not just the word, but the context in which it was used and the audio clip from the story.' Native audio is per-sentence with whole-episode playback.

verified_facts.claim: jpdb's word-state model and coverage percentages are the reference for highlighting
verified_facts.evidence: jpdb.io states/changelog: not-in-deck, due/failed, never-forget, suspended, blacklisted (with auto-blacklist options for particles and katakana loanwords). risks: Do not write an NHK News Web Easy fetcher. It is verifiably dead (301 -> HTTP 401 missing_token, no data embedded in index.html). Any tutorial or GitHub project you find describing news-list.json predates the NHK ONE migration. Even if someone finds a cookie-based workaround, NHK content is not openly licensed and cannot be bundled into a distributed app.

Do not strip Aozora's 《》 ruby markup. The naive `re.sub(r'《[^》]*》','')` throws away the single most valuable thing in the dataset — author-supplied, correct furigana. Convert it to <ruby><rt> instead. Also handle BOTH forms: the ｜-delimited form for kana-containing bases and the bare kanji-run form. Doing only one leaves stray 《》 in the output.

Do not skip the 文字遣い種別=='新字新仮名' filter on the Aozora index. Old-orthography works (旧字旧仮名) use pre-1946 spellings like ゐ, ゑ, けふ and old kanji forms such as 學/國. Shipping these to a beginner actively teaches wrong spellings that will be marked incorrect everywhere else.

Do not assume Aozora can supply N5 or N4 reading. I measured it: even the simplest 新美南吉 story sits at 46-72% N5+N4 kanji and 23-35 chars per sentence, far below the 95-98% lexical coverage the research says is needed. Bundling it at N5 produces exactly the dictionary-grinding misery that kills reading habits. Authoring N5/N4 texts is unavoidable work — budget for it.

Do not load kuromoji in the browser. The dictionary is ~17.8 MB gzipped across 12 files. On a phone over mobile data that is an app-killing first load, and it must be re-fetched if Cache Storage is evicted. Pre-tokenize at build time; the story JSON gets slightly bigger and the runtime gets dramatically smaller and faster.

Do not colour word states with background fills. Filled cells behind CJK glyphs destroy stroke legibility at phone font sizes, which is the opposite of what a reading app should do. Use 2px bottom borders. Reserve the background wash exclusively for the one transiently-tapped word.

Do not let the furigana toggle reflow the page. Ruby annotations add line height; toggling with display:none on <rt> collapses every line and throws the reader hundreds of pixels from where they were. Use visibility:hidden and a fixed line-height that always reserves the rt box.

Do not ship paragraph-level English translations. Sentence-level granularity is what makes reveal-on-tap pedagogically useful; paragraph-level lets the learner reconstruct the meaning without ever parsing the Japanese. And never lay JA and EN side by side in columns at 390px — stack them.

Do not gate business Japanese behind N1. This is the most common structural mistake in Japanese learning apps and it directly contradicts the user's stated goal. BJT J2 (420-530/800) is the employability bar, BJT 400+ is officially N2-equivalent for 2026 visas, and survival keigo is a closed set of fixed phrases learnable at N4. Run business as a parallel track from N4 or the user waits years for something they could use in months.

Do not teach keigo as isolated verb conjugations without the 内/外 social rule. A learner who can conjugate 尊敬語 perfectly but says 「田中部長はいらっしゃいません」 to a client has made a worse impression than one who used plain です/ます throughout. The register rule is the load-bearing part and it is invisible in JLPT material.

Do not present 了解しました and ご苦労様です as neutral synonyms of 承知しました and お疲れ様です. They are directional — peer/downward only — and using them upward is a real social error. Flag them with a warning in the data model (I included a `warn` field for this) and drill them as negative examples.

Do not bundle Hukumusume folk tales. They fetch fine (HTTP 200, and note they are UTF-8, NOT Shift_JIS like Aozora — a trap if you reuse the Aozora decoder) but the retellings are the site author's copyrighted prose and the terms page 404s. The public-domain 楠山正雄 folk-tale collection in the Aozora index covers the same ground legally.
Do not mirror tadoku.org's free PDFs or the Internet Archive graded readers. Free to read is not free to redistribute. Link out.

Do not promise unrealistic timelines. The official figures are 325-600 hours to N5 and 1600-2800 to N2 without a kanji background. A user told they will be fluent in three months quits in month four when they hit the well-documented N3-to-N2 difficulty spike. Publishing honest numbers with a live projection is a retention feature.

Do not use the GitHub REST releases API in the build script without auth. It rate-limited from this machine mid-session (403 'API rate limit exceeded'). Use the stable /releases/latest/download/<asset> redirect path instead, which worked (HTTP 200).

Web Speech API needs three guards or it ships broken: voices load asynchronously so you must handle the voiceschanged event, iOS requires the first utterance to fire inside a user-gesture handler, and if no ja-JP voice is present you must hide the speaker controls rather than let an English voice mangle Japanese.
